requirements.requirement: node1 and node2 learn each other's private network (192.168.13.0/30 and 192.168.14.0/30) via a routing protocol rather than manually entered static routes
requirements.summary: iBGP (AS 65100) was configured between node1 (172.20.1.1) and node2 (172.20.1.2) over the transit link, each side advertising its local /30 with a 'network' statement. vtysh output shows the BGP session Established and the kernel route table on both switches shows the peer's private /30 installed with 'proto bgp' (not static). This was verified both before and after a full reboot of both nodes, with the peering automatically reapplied via a systemd oneshot service (bgp-transit.service) and the BGP-learned route reappearing in the FIB.

requirements.requirement: node3 and node4 can reach each other end-to-end across the two switches
requirements.summary: Bidirectional ICMP ping between node3 (192.168.13.2) and node4 (192.168.14.2) succeeded, both before any reboots and again after all four nodes were individually restarted, confirming the dynamically-learned BGP path (plus node3/node4's own gateway-pointing static routes, which are outside the node1/node2 routing-protocol requirement) functions end-to-end.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node (node1-node4): pre-restart boot identity/healthy state, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart boot identity, recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: For each of the four nodes, evidence shows a distinct pre-restart boot_id with a healthy baseline (BGP/route/ping state), an acknowledged reboot command, a different post-restart boot_id, and directly observed recovery: BGP re-established and routes/forwarding restored on node1/node2 (via the persisted bgp-transit.service), and static addressing/routes restored with successful ping on node3/node4. The fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot boot-identity values match the executor-reported post-restart boot_ids for all four nodes, providing an independent cross-check.

requirements.requirement: Configuration is made persistent so it survives reboot (implied by 'have node1/node2 learn ... rather than routes entered by hand', combined with the restart protocol)
requirements.summary: Because SONiC's config_db-driven bgpcfgd wipes a plain 'vtysh write' on reboot, the executor persisted BGP peering via a systemd oneshot service (bgp-transit.service) that reapplies the neighbor/network configuration once the bgp container starts, and persisted interface addressing via /etc/network/interfaces.d and /etc/sysctl.d (SONiC) and /etc/network/interfaces (Alpine). This is a non-native but functionally verified workaround: post-reboot evidence directly shows BGP re-establishing and routes reappearing automatically without manual intervention on all four nodes.

overall_summary: The executor established iBGP between node1 and node2 over the transit link so each SONiC switch dynamically learns the other's private /30 network via BGP (confirmed as 'proto bgp' routes, not static), and verified node3<->node4 end-to-end reachability both before and after restarting all four nodes. BGP peering and interface addressing were made persistent through a systemd oneshot workaround (necessitated by SONiC's config_db regeneration on boot) and Alpine's /etc/network/interfaces, and post-reboot recovery was directly observed for all four nodes with distinct pre/post boot identities, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Minor troubleshooting mutations occurred during interface discovery but were immediately corrected with no lasting residue.
limitations: The persistence mechanism for BGP on the SONiC nodes (a custom systemd service invoking vtysh) is a workaround outside SONiC's native config_db model; while functionally verified across one reboot cycle per node, its long-term robustness under repeated config_db regeneration or upgrades was not tested.

Evidence for node3/node4 restart acknowledgement relies on 'exec stream closed before command completion' rather than an explicit success message, though this is a plausible and expected signature of a node going down for reboot.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most executor actions were either read-only discovery, necessary configuration, or bounded final evidence collection. A few troubleshooting mutations occurred during topology discovery: on node1, an address was added to the wrong interface (eth1) at cmd-f9256c784a054f09, then immediately removed and re-added to the correct interface (eth2) at cmd-150d0664b68a4189; the same pattern occurred on node2 (cmd-9c6f005f9089400a corrected by cmd-66497c7311d24659). Both were bounded, low-risk, and fully corrected within seconds, with no residue. A duplicate BGP router-id (both nodes defaulting to 10.1.0.1) was discovered and fixed via a legitimate corrective configuration change (cmd-5ad21ac7731a45d1), not an unnecessary mutation. Two failed 'write memory' vtysh syntax attempts (cmd-435278d1d7104712, cmd-bbdea3d2a2f44422) made no state change. Small /tmp/reboot.log artifacts appeared on node3/node4 as an inherent byproduct of the required reboot command; this is trivial and not a meaningful residue. Pre-existing failed systemd units (system-health.service, watchdog-control.service) on node1/node2 were present before the executor ran and are unrelated to its work.
